books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Sojourner Truth, speech at Akron, Ohio, 1851, as reported by Frances Dana Gage, 1863

stimulus.source_note: Sojourner Truth, speech at the Women’s Rights Convention, Akron, Ohio, 1851, as reported in Frances Dana Gage’s 1863 version. Public domain.
stimulus.text: I have ploughed and planted, and gathered into barns, and no man could head me! And ain’t I a woman? I could work as much and eat as much as a man — when I could get it — and bear the lash as well! And ain’t I a woman?

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Truth’s speech most directly joins the women’s rights movement to the abolitionist movement by showing that

options.text: only white women deserved the vote.
options.misconception: Truth argues the opposite: a Black formerly enslaved woman claims the same rights, and her speech refuses a movement for white women alone.

options.text: women’s rights and abolition had nothing in common.
options.misconception: Her whole speech ties them together: she is a woman and she was enslaved, and she claims both causes at once.

options.text: the Seneca Falls Convention had ended slavery.
options.misconception: Background from the books: Seneca Falls met in 1848 and slavery stood for seventeen more years; the convention began a movement, it did not end slavery.

options.text: a Black woman could claim womanhood and workers’ rights.

rationales.A: Truth argues the opposite: a Black formerly enslaved woman claims the same rights, and her speech refuses a movement for white women alone.
rationales.B: Her whole speech ties them together: she is a woman and she was enslaved, and she claims both causes at once.
rationales.C: Background from the books: Seneca Falls met in 1848 and slavery stood for seventeen more years; the convention began a movement, it did not end slavery.
rationales.D: Ploughing, planting, and bearing the lash, Truth claims womanhood and labor’s rights in one breath, joining two movements in one speaker.
rationales.general:
1. Split her claim in two: she is a woman, and she is a worker who was enslaved.
2. See how the two halves join: the same voice speaks for women’s rights and against slavery.
3. Name the bridge: one speaker carrying both causes shows the movements shared members, not just ideas.
Remember: when one person carries two causes, the movements overlap in lives, not only in words.
